## AP Biology

AP Biology explores the living world at every scale, from molecular processes to ecosystem dynamics. The course is organised around four Big Ideas: evolution, energetics, information transfer, and systems interactions. You will study biochemistry, cell structure and function, genetics and gene expression, evolution and phylogeny, ecology, and animal physiology.

Key topics include the chemistry of life, enzyme kinetics, cellular respiration and photosynthesis, Mendelian and molecular genetics, population genetics, and biological systems. The exam tests both conceptual understanding and data analysis, so practise interpreting graphs, designing experiments, and applying the scientific method.

Read the full guide: [AP Biology Study Guide](/biology/).

## AP Chemistry

AP Chemistry gives you a deep understanding of matter and its interactions. The course covers atomic structure and periodicity, chemical bonding and molecular geometry, intermolecular forces, chemical reactions, stoichiometry, thermodynamics, kinetics, equilibrium, acids and bases, electrochemistry, and nuclear chemistry.

You will work with Lewis structures, VSEPR theory, ideal gas laws, and equilibrium calculations. The exam rewards both conceptual clarity and quantitative problem-solving. Practise balancing half-reactions, constructing Born-Haber cycles, and interpreting titration curves.

Read the full guide: [AP Chemistry Study Guide](/chemistry/).

## AP Computer Science A

AP Computer Science A teaches object-oriented programming in Java. Core topics include classes and objects, inheritance and polymorphism, arrays and ArrayLists, sorting and searching algorithms, recursion, and basic data structures. The course emphasises algorithmic thinking and the ability to read, write, and analyse code.

You will practise designing classes, implementing methods, tracing code execution, and analysing time complexity. The exam tests your ability to write correct Java code and reason about program behaviour.

Read the full guide: [AP Computer Science A Study Guide](/ap-computer-science-a/).

## AP Computer Science Principles

AP Computer Science Principles introduces the foundational ideas of computing without requiring a specific programming language. Topics include the internet, data, cybersecurity, algorithms, programming, abstraction, and the social impact of computing.

The course builds computational thinking through creative problem-solving and the exploration of real-world computing applications. You will complete a Create Performance Task as part of the course.

Read the full guide: [AP Computer Science Principles Study Guide](/ap-computer-science-principles/).

## AP English Language and Composition

AP English Language and Composition focuses on rhetorical analysis, argumentation, and synthesis. You will analyse non-fiction texts, construct evidence-based arguments, and write persuasive essays. The course develops your ability to evaluate how authors use language to persuade and inform.

The exam includes multiple-choice questions on prose passages and three free-response essays: synthesis, rhetorical analysis, and argumentation.

## AP English Literature and Composition

AP English Literature and Composition centres on close reading and literary analysis. You will study fiction, poetry, and drama, analysing how authors use literary elements such as imagery, symbolism, characterisation, and narrative structure. The course trains you to construct interpretive arguments grounded in textual evidence.

The exam includes multiple-choice questions on prose and poetry passages and three free-response essays: literary analysis, prose analysis, and poetry analysis.

## AP History

The AP History programme includes three distinct courses, each with its own thematic focus:

### AP United States History

AP US History covers American history from 1491 to the present. Topics include colonial societies, the American Revolution, the Constitution, westward expansion, the Civil War and Reconstruction, industrialisation, the Progressive Era, the World Wars, the Cold War, and contemporary America. You will practise document-based questions (DBQs), long essay questions, and short answer questions.

Read the full guide: [AP History Study Guide](/history/).

### AP European History

AP European History traces European civilisation from 1450 to the present. Key themes include the Renaissance, the Reformation, absolutism, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, industrialisation, nationalism, the World Wars, the Cold War, and contemporary Europe. The exam tests your ability to analyse primary sources and construct historical arguments.

### AP World History: Modern

AP World History covers global history from 1200 CE to the present. The course emphasises comparison, causation, and continuity and change over time across Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. You will analyse trade networks, empires, revolutions, and globalisation.

## AP Mathematics

### AP Calculus AB

AP Calculus AB covers differential and integral calculus. Topics include limits, continuity, derivatives, applications of derivatives, integrals, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and applications of integration. The course emphasises conceptual understanding and the ability to solve problems analytically, graphically, and numerically.

Read the full guide: [AP Calculus AB Study Guide](/calculus-ab/).

Practice materials: [AP Calculus AB Practice](/practice-calculus-ab/).

### AP Calculus BC

AP Calculus BC includes all of the Calculus AB content plus additional topics: sequences, series, parametric equations, polar coordinates, and the Taylor and Maclaurin series. The course provides a more rigorous treatment of integration techniques and infinite processes.

Practice materials: [AP Calculus BC Practice](/practice-calculus/).

### AP Statistics

AP Statistics introduces statistical reasoning and data analysis. Topics include exploratory data analysis, sampling and experimental design, probability distributions, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and regression. You will practise interpreting real data sets, constructing statistical arguments, and using technology for calculations.

Read the full guide: [AP Statistics Study Guide](/statistics/).

## AP Physics

AP Physics offers several levels of study:

### AP Physics 1: Algebra-Based

AP Physics 1 covers Newtonian mechanics, work, energy, power, mechanical waves, sound, and introductory circuits. The course uses algebra and trigonometry rather than calculus. You will analyse physical systems, design experiments, and make predictions based on physical laws.

Read the full guide: [AP Physics 1 Study Guide](/physics-1/).

Practice materials: [AP Physics Mechanics Practice](/practice-physics-mechanics/).

### AP Physics 2: Algebra-Based

AP Physics 2 extends into fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, electricity and magnetism, optics, and modern physics including atomic and nuclear physics. The course builds on the conceptual framework of Physics 1 with more advanced topics.

### AP Physics C: Mechanics

AP Physics C: Mechanics is a calculus-based course covering kinematics, Newton's laws, work and energy, systems of particles and linear momentum, rotation, oscillations, and gravitation. The course provides a rigorous treatment of classical mechanics.

### AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism

AP Physics C: E&M covers electrostatics, conductors and capacitors, electric circuits, magnetic fields, and electromagnetism. The course uses calculus to derive and apply physical laws.

Read the full guide: [AP Physics Study Guide](/physics/).

## AP Exam Strategy Tips

Success on AP exams requires more than content knowledge. Here are proven strategies:

### Before the Exam

1. **Start early.** Begin reviewing at least six to eight weeks before the exam. Spaced repetition and consistent practice outperform last-minute cramming.
2. **Use the College Board's course description.** The Course and Exam Description (CED) is the definitive source for what content appears on the exam. Study it carefully and identify any gaps.
3. **Practise with released exams.** The College Board publishes past exams with scoring guidelines. These are the closest thing to the real test and help you calibrate your timing and depth of response.
4. **Make a formula and equation sheet.** Even if the exam provides a formula sheet, writing your own helps you memorise and understand the relationships between quantities.

### During the Exam

1. **Read every question carefully.** Many mistakes come from misreading what the question is asking. Underline key terms and identify the specific skill being tested.
2. **Manage your time.** Allocate time proportionally to the number of points each question is worth. If you get stuck, move on and return later.
3. **Show your work.** On free-response questions, partial credit is awarded for correct reasoning even if the final answer is wrong. Write down every step.
4. **Use process of elimination.** On multiple-choice questions, eliminate obviously wrong answers before guessing. This increases your probability of selecting the correct option.
5. **Answer every question.** There is no penalty for wrong answers on AP exams. Never leave a question blank.

### After the Exam

1. **Review your performance.** If you have access to your score report, identify weak areas and use them to guide future study.
2. **Consider score reports for universities.** Send your AP scores to universities that grant credit. A score of 4 or 5 typically earns credit, though policies vary.
3. **Build on your AP foundation.** AP courses prepare you for university-level work. Continue building on the skills and knowledge you have developed.

## Cross-Curricular Connections

AP courses do not exist in isolation. The knowledge you gain in one subject often supports success in others:

- **[GCSE Resources](https://gcse.wyattau.com)**, If you are transitioning from the GCSE system, these resources bridge the gap between GCSE and AP-level study.
- **[IB Resources](https://ib.wyattau.com)**, The IB programme shares many topics with AP. Compare approaches and deepen your understanding across both curricula.
- **[SAT Preparation](https://sat.wyattau.com)**, The SAT tests reading, writing, and mathematics skills that underpin AP success. Strengthen your foundations with SAT prep.
- **[Mathematics](https://mathematics.wyattau.com)**, University-level mathematics extends the calculus and statistics covered in AP.
- **[Physics](https://physics.wyattau.com)**, University physics deepens the mechanics, electricity, and magnetism taught in AP Physics.
- **[Chemistry](https://chemistry.wyattau.com)**, University chemistry builds on the atomic structure, bonding, and reactions covered in AP Chemistry.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many AP exams should I take?

There is no single right number. Focus on quality over quantity. Take AP courses in subjects you are genuinely interested in and where you can perform well. One or two well-prepared AP exams are more valuable than five rushed ones. Consider your overall workload, extracurricular commitments, and university goals.

### What score do I need to earn college credit?

Most universities award credit for scores of 4 or 5, though some accept scores of 3. Policies vary widely by institution and department. Check the specific university's AP credit policy before registering for exams. Elite universities may grant credit only for scores of 5 or may place you into advanced courses rather than awarding credit.

### When should I start preparing for AP exams?

Ideally, begin preparing when you enrol in the AP course. Consistent study throughout the year is far more effective than cramming in the spring. If you are self-studying for an AP exam, start at least four to six months before the exam date.

### Can I self-study for AP exams?

Yes. The College Board allows anyone to register for AP exams, regardless of whether they are enrolled in an AP course. Self-study requires discipline and a clear study plan. Use the course description as your roadmap, obtain a good textbook, and practise with released exams.

### How do AP exams compare to IB exams?

AP exams are subject-specific and test content knowledge and analytical skills within a single discipline. IB exams are part of a broader diploma programme that includes internal assessments, an extended essay, and Theory of Knowledge. Both are rigorous, but they differ in structure and philosophy. Many students take both depending on their school's offerings.

### Are AP courses worth it for university admissions?

AP courses demonstrate academic rigour and college readiness. Admissions committees view AP coursework favourably, especially when you perform well. However, AP courses are only one component of your application. Strong grades, test scores, extracurricular activities, and essays all matter. Take AP courses where you can excel, not just to fill a transcript.

### What is the difference between AP Calculus AB and BC?

Calculus AB covers differential and integral calculus at a foundational level. Calculus BC includes all AB content plus sequences, series, parametric equations, polar coordinates, and more advanced integration techniques. Calculus BC is more demanding and covers about 60% more material. If you have a strong数学 background, BC may be the better choice, but AB provides a solid foundation for most STEM majors.

### How do I handle AP exam stress?

Start preparing early to reduce last-minute pressure. Break your study plan into manageable daily tasks. Practise under timed conditions to build confidence. Get adequate sleep before the exam. Remember that a single exam score does not define your academic potential. Use study groups, office hours, and online resources when you need support.

## Common Mistakes

**Treating AP courses as easy alternatives to university courses:** AP exams cover college-level material and require serious preparation. The pass rate for AP Calculus BC is roughly 40% for scores of 5, nearly 60% of students score 3 or below. Underestimating the difficulty leads to inadequate preparation.

**Focusing on test-taking strategies without understanding concepts:** AP exams increasingly test conceptual understanding and application, not just rote memorisation. Knowing the chain rule formula is insufficient, you must understand when and why to apply it in novel contexts. Conceptual gaps become exposed on the free-response sections.

**Neglecting to practise with official College Board materials:** Third-party practice tests may not match the style, difficulty, or content emphasis of actual AP exams. Always use official released exams and scoring guidelines to calibrate your preparation and understand what graders expect.

## Cross-References

- **[Site Home](../../):** Main landing page for ap notes.
- **Practice:** Practice problems for revision.

## Intuition

AP courses are designed to be the equivalent of first-year university courses, they are not lighter versions of college classes but condensed versions that demand the same depth of understanding in less time. The key to succeeding in AP is recognising that the exam tests **conceptual understanding and application**, not rote memorisation. You can memorise every formula for AP Calculus, but if you cannot explain *why* the chain rule works or apply it to a novel problem, you will struggle on the free-response questions.

The subjects covered here, Calculus, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Statistics, History, English, and Computer Science, share a common structure: foundational concepts build on each other sequentially, and gaps in early material compound later. This means you cannot afford to skip topics you find difficult. The practice problems and flashcards in these notes are designed to build the kind of understanding that lets you transfer knowledge between contexts, which is exactly what AP exams reward.

Approach your AP study with active recall (attempt problems before reading explanations), spaced repetition (revisit difficult material after increasing intervals), and interleaving (mix topics rather than studying one to completion). These evidence-based strategies are far more effective than re-reading notes or highlighting. The goal is not just to pass the AP exam but to build a foundation of understanding that will serve you in university and beyond.

## Overview

The Advanced Placement (AP) program, administered by the College Board, allows US high school
Students to take college-level courses and earn credit or advanced standing at many universities. AP
Exams are scored on a scale of 1 to 5, with most colleges granting credit for scores of 3 or higher.

## Subjects Covered

These notes align to the AP Course and Exam Descriptions (CEDs) and cover the following subjects:

- **AP Calculus AB/BC** -- Limits, derivatives, integrals, differential equations, and sequences and
  series (BC only). See
  [Limits and Continuity](/maths/1-limits-and-continuity/1_limits-and-continuity/).
- **AP Physics 1/2/C** -- Mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, fluids, and modern physics.
  See [Kinematics](/physics/1-kinematics/1_kinematics/).
- **AP Chemistry** -- Atomic structure, bonding, stoichiometry, thermodynamics, kinetics, and
  equilibrium. See
  [Atomic Structure and Periodicity](/chemistry/1-atomic-structure-and-periodicity/1_atomic-structure-and-periodicity/).
- **AP Biology** -- Biochemistry, cell biology, energetics, genetics, and evolution. See
  [Chemistry of Life](/biology/1-chemistry-of-life/1_chemistry-of-life/).
- **AP Computer Science A/Principles** -- Programming in Java, algorithms, data structures,
  abstraction, and the internet. See
  [Computational Thinking](/computer-science/1-computational-thinking/1_computational-thinking/).

## Exam Structure

Each AP exam consists of two sections:

1. **Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQ)** -- ~50% of the score, 60 questions, 90 minutes.
2. **Free-Response Questions (FRQ)** -- ~50% of the score, 4-6 questions, 90 minutes.

The FRQ section requires detailed written responses showing all work, reasoning, and justification.
These notes emphasize the conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills needed for both
Sections.

- Each topic references the relevant CED units where applicable.
- Worked examples demonstrate the full reasoning expected on FRQs.
- Common Pitfalls sections highlight frequent exam errors.
- Practice questions are included at the end of each topic.

## AP Physics 1 Study Guide

Comprehensive study guide for AP Physics 1 (Algebra-Based), aligned with the College Board Course
and Exam Description. Covers mechanics and rotational motion with emphasis on conceptual
understanding and problem-solving.

## 1. Kinematics

### Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration

| Quantity     | Type   | Definition                           | SI Unit |
| ------------ | ------ | ------------------------------------ | ------- |
| Displacement | Vector | Change in position, $\Delta \vec{r}$ | m       |
| Distance     | Scalar | Total path length                    | m       |
| Velocity     | Vector | Rate of change of displacement       | m/s     |
| Speed        | Scalar | Rate of change of distance           | m/s     |
| Acceleration | Vector | Rate of change of velocity           | m/s$^2$ |

### One-Dimensional Kinematics

**Constant acceleration equations:**

$$
v = v_0 + at
$$

$$
x = x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2
$$

$$
v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)
$$

$$
x = x_0 + \frac{1}{2}(v_0 + v)t
$$

### Two-Dimensional Motion

In 2D, resolve all vectors into perpendicular components. The $x$ and $y$ components of motion are
independent of each other (superposition principle).

### Projectile Motion

For a projectile launched with initial speed $v_0$ at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal (ignoring
air resistance):

$$
v_{0x} = v_0 \cos\theta, \quad v_{0y} = v_0 \sin\theta
$$

**Horizontal (constant velocity):**

$$
x(t) = v_{0x}\, t
$$

**Vertical (constant acceleration $a_y = -g$):**

$$
y(t) = v_{0y}\, t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2
$$

$$
v_y(t) = v_{0y} - gt
$$

**Time of flight:** $t = \dfrac{2v_{0y}}{g}$

**Maximum height:** $H = \dfrac{v_{0y}^2}{2g}$

**Range:** $R = \dfrac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$

### Free Fall

An object in free fall experiences only the force of gravity. All objects in free fall have the same
acceleration $g \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ near Earth"s surface, regardless of mass.

### Graphical Analysis

- **Position-time graph:** Slope gives velocity
- **Velocity-time graph:** Slope gives acceleration; area under the curve gives displacement
- **Acceleration-time graph:** Area under the curve gives change in velocity

## 2. Dynamics

### Newton's Laws

**First Law (Inertia):** An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion
with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by a net external force.

**Second Law:** The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration:

$$
\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\vec{a}
$$

This is a vector equation, apply separately in each direction.

**Third Law:** For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. Forces always
come in pairs acting on different objects.

### Free-Body Diagrams

1. Isolate the object of interest
2. Draw arrows for every force acting **on** the object
3. Forces act **on** the object; the object's forces act on other things
4. Common forces: weight ($mg$), normal force ($N$), tension ($T$), friction ($f$), applied force
   ($F$)

### Friction

**Static friction:** $f_s \leq \mu_s N$ (prevents motion; maximum value is $\mu_s N$)

**Kinetic friction:** $f_k = \mu_k N$ (opposes motion; constant magnitude)

where $\mu_s$ and $\mu_k$ are coefficients of static and kinetic friction respectively, and $N$ is
the normal force.

### Inclined Planes

On an incline at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal:

$$
a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k \cos\theta)
$$

The component of weight parallel to the plane is $mg\sin\theta$; the component perpendicular (which
equals the normal force) is $mg\cos\theta$.

### Atwood Machine

Two masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_2 > m_1$) connected by a string over a frictionless pulley:

$$
a = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}
$$

$$
T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}
$$

### Uniform Circular Motion

An object moving in a circle of radius $r$ at constant speed $v$ has a centripetal acceleration
directed towards the centre:

$$
a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}
$$

The net inward force providing this acceleration is:

$$
F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r
$$

where $\omega$ is the angular velocity in rad/s.

### Gravitational Force

Newton's law of universal gravitation:

$$
F_g = \frac{Gm_1 m_2}{r^2}
$$

where $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$.

The gravitational field strength at distance $r$ from mass $M$:

$$
g = \frac{GM}{r^2}
$$

## 3. Work and Energy

### Work

Work done by a constant force:

$$
W = Fd\cos\theta
$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Work is positive when the force
has a component in the direction of displacement and negative when opposing displacement.

For a variable force:

$$
W = \int_a^b F(x)\, dx
$$

### Work-Energy Theorem

The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

$$
W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i
$$

### Kinetic Energy

$$
K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2
$$

### Potential Energy

**Gravitational potential energy (near Earth's surface):**

$$
U_g = mgh
$$

**Elastic (spring) potential energy:**

$$
U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2
$$

where $k$ is the spring constant and $x$ is the displacement from equilibrium.

### Conservation of Energy

In the absence of non-conservative forces (e.g., friction):

$$
K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f
$$

When friction is present:

$$
K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f + E_{\text{lost to friction}}
$$

where $E_{\text{lost to friction}} = f_k d$.

### Power

Average power is the rate at which work is done:

$$
P = \frac{W}{\Delta t}
$$

Instantaneous power:

$$
P = Fv\cos\theta
$$

SI unit: watt (W), where $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$.

## 4. Momentum

### Impulse and Linear Momentum

**Momentum:**

$$
\vec{p} = m\vec{v}
$$

**Impulse:**

$$
\vec{J} = \vec{F}_{\text{avg}}\,\Delta t = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i
$$

The impulse-momentum theorem states that the impulse on an object equals its change in momentum.
Graphically, impulse equals the area under a force-time graph.

### Conservation of Momentum

When the net external force on a system is zero, the total momentum of the system is conserved:

$$
m_1\vec{v}_{1i} + m_2\vec{v}_{2i} = m_1\vec{v}_{1f} + m_2\vec{v}_{2f}
$$

This applies independently to each component direction.

### Collisions

**Elastic collision:** Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

For a 1D elastic collision between masses $m_1$ and $m_2$:

$$
v_{1f} = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)v_{1i} + 2m_2 v_{2i}}{m_1 + m_2}
$$

$$
v_{2f} = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)v_{2i} + 2m_1 v_{1i}}{m_1 + m_2}
$$

**Inelastic collision:** Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.

**Perfectly inelastic collision:** The objects stick together after collision.

$$
(m_1 + m_2)v_f = m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i}
$$

### Centre of Mass

The centre of mass of a system of particles:

$$
x_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + \cdots}{m_1 + m_2 + \cdots}
$$

The centre of mass of a system moves as if all external forces act on a single particle of total
mass located at the centre of mass.

## 5. Rotational Motion

### Torque

Torque is the rotational analogue of force:

$$
\tau = rF\sin\theta = r_\perp F
$$

where $r_\perp = r\sin\theta$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of
action of the force (the moment arm). Positive torque causes counter-clockwise rotation; negative
causes clockwise.

Net torque and angular acceleration:

$$
\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha
$$

where $I$ is the rotational inertia and $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration.

### Rotational Inertia (Moment of Inertia)

$$
I = \sum m_i r_i^2
$$

For continuous objects: $I = \int r^2\, dm$

Common moments of inertia:

| Object                                    | Rotational Inertia  |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| Solid disc/cylinder (axis through centre) | $\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$  |
| Hoop/ring (axis through centre)           | $MR^2$              |
| Solid sphere                              | $\dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$  |
| Thin rod (axis through centre)            | $\dfrac{1}{12}ML^2$ |
| Thin rod (axis through end)               | $\dfrac{1}{3}ML^2$  |
| Point mass at distance $r$                | $mr^2$              |

### Angular Momentum

$$
L = I\omega
$$

For a point mass: $L = mvr_\perp$

**Conservation of angular momentum:** When no net external torque acts on a system, $I\omega$ is
constant:

$$
I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f
$$

### Rotational Kinetic Energy

$$
K_r = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2
$$

Total kinetic energy for a rolling object:

$$
K_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2
$$

### Rolling Motion

For an object rolling without slipping:

$$
v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega
$$

$$
a_{\text{cm}} = R\alpha
$$

Acceleration of a solid sphere rolling down an incline of angle $\theta$:

$$
a = \frac{5}{7}g\sin\theta
$$

## 6. Oscillations

### Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)

An object undergoes SHM when a restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium:

$$
F = -kx
$$

This yields sinusoidal motion:

$$
x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)
$$

where $A$ is the amplitude, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, and $\phi$ is the phase constant.

### Mass-Spring System

$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}, \quad T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \quad f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}
$$

where $T$ is the period (time for one complete oscillation) and $f$ is the frequency.

### Simple Pendulum

For small angles ($\theta < 15°$), a simple pendulum approximates SHM:

$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}, \quad T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}, \quad f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}
$$

Note: the period of a pendulum is independent of mass.

### Energy in SHM

Total mechanical energy is conserved and constant:

$$
E_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = K_{\text{max}} = U_{\text{max}}
$$

At any position $x$:

$$
K = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2), \quad U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2
$$

### Period and Frequency

$$
T = \frac{1}{f}, \quad f = \frac{1}{T}, \quad \omega = 2\pi f = \frac{2\pi}{T}
$$

## 7. Key Equations

### Kinematics

$$
v = v_0 + at \quad x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 \quad v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x
$$

$$
x_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g} \quad R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}
$$

### Dynamics

$$
F_{\text{net}} = ma \quad f_k = \mu_k N \quad F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}
$$

### Energy

$$
K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \quad U_g = mgh \quad U_s = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2
$$

$$
W = Fd\cos\theta \quad P = \frac{W}{\Delta t} = Fv\cos\theta
$$

### Momentum

$$
p = mv \quad J = F_{\text{avg}}\,\Delta t = \Delta p
$$

### Rotation

$$
\tau = I\alpha \quad L = I\omega \quad K_r = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2
$$

### Oscillations

$$
T_{\text{spring}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} \quad T_{\text{pendulum}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}
$$

## 8. Exam Tips

1. **Draw a free-body diagram for every problem.** It earns points, organises your thinking, and
   helps identify all forces. Never skip this step on the free-response section.
2. **Check dimensions and units at every step.** If your answer has units of kg·m/s when you expect
   joules, there is an error. Dimensional analysis catches many mistakes quickly.
3. **Define your coordinate system.** State which direction is positive and where the origin is.
   This prevents sign errors and makes your reasoning clear to the grader.
4. **Distinguish between vector and scalar quantities.** Displacement is not distance; velocity is
   not speed. The AP exam frequently tests this distinction.
5. **Apply conservation laws first.** Before writing out Newton's second law for every object, check
   whether conservation of energy or momentum solves the problem more efficiently.
6. **Explain your reasoning in words.** The AP Physics 1 exam emphasises conceptual understanding.
   After writing equations, explain what each term represents and why the equation applies.
7. **Use graphs to support your answers.** The exam often asks you to sketch or interpret graphs.
   Practise translating between equations, graphs, and physical descriptions.

## 9. Common Mistakes

1. **Confusing mass and weight.** Mass is an intrinsic property measured in kg; weight is the
   gravitational force $mg$ measured in newtons. An object has the same mass on the Moon but
   different weight.
2. **Including internal forces in $\vec{F}_{\text{net}}$.** Only external forces contribute to the
   net force on a system. The tension in a rope between two parts of the same system is an internal
   force and cancels out.
3. **Forgetting the normal force is not always $mg$.** On an incline, $N = mg\cos\theta$. In an
   accelerating lift, $N = m(g \pm a)$. Always derive $N$ from Newton's second law.
4. **Mixing up centripetal and centrifugal forces.** "Centrifugal force" is a fictitious force that
   appears in a rotating reference frame. In an inertial frame, only the centripetal force (directed
   towards the centre) acts on the object.
5. **Using the wrong collision formula.** Only use elastic collision equations when kinetic energy
   is conserved. For perfectly inelastic collisions, use conservation of momentum alone and set
   final velocities equal.
6. **Incorrect rotational inertia.** Do not assume $I = MR^2$ for all objects. A solid disc has
   $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$; a solid sphere has $I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$. Know the common values.
7. **Applying the small-angle approximation outside its range.** The pendulum formula
   $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ only holds for angles below roughly 15°. For larger amplitudes, the period
   is longer.

## 10. Summary

| Topic             | Key Ideas                                                                               |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Kinematics        | Displacement, velocity, acceleration, projectile motion, free fall, motion graphs       |
| Dynamics          | Newton's three laws, free-body diagrams, friction, inclined planes, circular motion     |
| Work and Energy   | Work, work-energy theorem, kinetic/potential energy, conservation of energy, power      |
| Momentum          | Impulse-momentum theorem, conservation of momentum, elastic and inelastic collisions    |
| Rotational Motion | Torque, rotational inertia, angular momentum, conservation of angular momentum, rolling |
| Oscillations      | SHM, mass-spring systems, pendulums, energy in oscillations                             |

AP Physics 1 rewards deep conceptual understanding over memorisation. Focus on building physical
intuition, ask yourself _why_ an object behaves as it does before reaching for an equation.
Practise explaining your reasoning evidently in writing, as the free-response section heavily
weights qualitative explanations alongside quantitative solutions.

## Intuition

AP Physics 1 is the **algebra-based introduction to mechanics**, it describes how objects move and why. The course builds from kinematics (describing motion) through forces (causing motion) to energy and momentum (conservation laws that simplify complex problems).

**The physics chain:** Kinematics describes _what_ happens. Newton's laws explain _why_ it happens. Energy and momentum provide _shortcut methods_ that bypass detailed force analysis. Rotational motion extends all these ideas to spinning objects. The key is recognising which approach, forces, energy, or momentum, is simplest for each problem.

**Conceptual understanding over calculation:** AP Physics 1 emphasises reasoning about physical situations. Can you predict what happens when you cut a string? Can you explain _why_ a ball rolls slower than it slides? The exam tests your ability to justify answers, not just compute numbers.

**The power of free-body diagrams:** Nearly every mechanics problem starts with a free-body diagram. Isolate the object, identify every force, and resolve into components. This single step solves 80% of mechanics problems.

## Common Pitfalls

- Confusing terminology or concepts that appear similar but have distinct meanings.
- Overlooking key assumptions or boundary conditions that limit applicability.

**Common Mistakes:**

- Confusing the limit value with the function value
- Forgetting to check both left-hand and right-hand limits

## AP Calculus AB -- Practice

16 MCQ practice problems. Select an answer, submit, and review the explanation.

---

### Limits and Continuity

Limits are the foundation of calculus. Before you can differentiate or integrate, you need to understand what happens to a function as the input approaches a value, even if the function is undefined there. The key intuition is that limits describe **behaviour near a point**, not behaviour at the point.

**Common limit patterns to recognise:**

- $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$ is the definition of $f'(a)$
- $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ (the most important trigonometric limit)
- $\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right)^x = e$ (the definition of $e$)

**When L'Hopital's rule applies:** Only when the limit produces $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$. Always verify the indeterminate form first.

**Common Mistakes:**

- Applying L'Hopital's rule without verifying the indeterminate form first
- Forgetting that limits describe behaviour *near* a point, not *at* the point
- Confusing $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ with $f(a) = L$

---

### Derivatives

The derivative measures the **instantaneous rate of change** of a function. Geometrically, it is the slope of the tangent line. The power rule, product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule are your computational tools, but understanding *why* the chain rule works (composition of functions) matters more than memorising the formula.

**The chain rule in plain English:** If $y$ depends on $u$, and $u$ depends on $x$, then the rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ is the product of the individual rates: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}$.

**Common Mistakes:**

- Forgetting the chain rule when differentiating composite functions
- Confusing the product rule $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ with the quotient rule
- Applying the power rule to functions like $e^x$ or $\sin x$

---

### Integrals

Integration is the reverse of differentiation, but its deeper meaning is **accumulation**. The definite integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ sums up infinitesimal contributions of $f(x)$ over the interval $[a, b]$. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects the two branches: differentiation and integration are inverse operations.

**Common integration strategies:**

- **u-substitution:** Use when you see a function and its derivative together
- **Integration by parts:** Use for products of different types of functions (polynomial × exponential, polynomial × trig)
- **Recognise special forms:** $\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C$, $\int e^x\,dx = e^x + C$

**Common Mistakes:**

- Forgetting the constant of integration $+C$ on indefinite integrals
- Incorrectly applying u-substitution (wrong $du$ or wrong limits)
- Confusing definite and indefinite integrals

---

### Differential Equations

Differential equations describe how quantities change in relation to each other. The most common type on the AP exam is **separation of variables**: rearrange the equation so all $y$ terms are on one side and all $x$ terms on the other, then integrate both sides. Exponential growth and decay ($\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$) and logistic growth ($\frac{dy}{dt} = ky(1 - y/L)$) are the models you must know.

**Common Mistakes:**

- Forgetting to separate variables before integrating
- Mixing up exponential growth ($k > 0$) and decay ($k < 0$)
- Incorrectly applying initial conditions to find the constant $C$

## AP Physics C -- Mechanics Practice

16 MCQ practice problems. Select an answer, submit, and review the explanation.

### Kinematics

**Intuition:** Kinematics is the geometry of motion. It describes *how* objects move (trajectory, velocity, acceleration) without worrying about *why* they move (forces).

**Common Mistakes:**

- Confusing displacement (vector) with distance (scalar)
- Using kinematic equations for non-constant acceleration
- Forgetting that velocity and acceleration can have opposite signs

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" questions={practiceQuestions} />

## Free-Response Practice Problems

### Problem 1: Projectile Motion with Air Resistance (15 points)

A projectile of mass $m$ is launched from the origin with initial speed $v_0$ at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. Assume air resistance is proportional to velocity: $\mathbf{F}_{\text{drag}} = -b\mathbf{v}$.

**(a)** Write the differential equations of motion for the $x$ and $y$ components. (4 points)

**(b)** For the case $b = 0$ (no air resistance), derive expressions for the time of flight, maximum height, and range. (6 points)

**(c)** Explain qualitatively how air resistance affects each of these quantities. (3 points)

**(d)** If $b$ is small, suggest an approximation method to find the corrected range. (2 points)

**Solution:**

**(a)** The equations of motion are:
$$m\frac{dv_x}{dt} = -bv_x \implies \frac{dv_x}{dt} = -\frac{b}{m}v_x$$

$$m\frac{dv_y}{dt} = -mg - bv_y \implies \frac{dv_y}{dt} = -g - \frac{b}{m}v_y$$

**(b)** Without air resistance:

- Time of flight: $T = \frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$
- Maximum height: $H = \frac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$
- Range: $R = \frac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$

**(c)** Air resistance:

- Reduces time of flight (projectile decelerates faster)
- Reduces maximum height (energy is lost to drag)
- Reduces range (both horizontal and vertical motion are affected)

**(d)** Perturbation theory: expand the solution in powers of $b/m$ and solve order by order.

**Scoring rubric:**

- Part (a): 2 points for each correct differential equation
- Part (b): 2 points each for correct expressions
- Part (c): 1 point for each correct qualitative effect
- Part (d): 2 points for mentioning perturbation theory

---

### Problem 2: Rotational Dynamics (15 points)

A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is placed on a rough inclined plane at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction is $\mu_s$.

**(a)** Draw a free-body diagram showing all forces acting on the cylinder. (3 points)

**(b)** Write the equations for translational and rotational motion. (4 points)

**(c)** Derive the condition for the cylinder to roll without slipping. (4 points)

**(d)** Find the minimum angle $\theta_{\text{min}}$ at which the cylinder begins to slip. (4 points)

**Solution:**

**(a)** Forces: weight $Mg$ downward, normal force $N$ perpendicular to incline, friction $f$ up the incline (provides torque for rolling).

**(b)** Translation along incline: $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$

Translation perpendicular: $N - Mg\cos\theta = 0$

Rotation: $\tau = fR = I\alpha$

Rolling condition: $a = R\alpha$

**(c)** For a solid cylinder, $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$.

From torque equation: $fR = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 \cdot \frac{a}{R} \implies f = \frac{1}{2}Ma$

Substituting into translation equation:
$$Mg\sin\theta - \frac{1}{2}Ma = Ma \implies a = \frac{2g\sin\theta}{3}$$

$$f = \frac{1}{2}M \cdot \frac{2g\sin\theta}{3} = \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{3}$$

Rolling without slipping requires $f \leq \mu_s N = \mu_s Mg\cos\theta$:
$$\frac{Mg\sin\theta}{3} \leq \mu_s Mg\cos\theta \implies \tan\theta \leq 3\mu_s$$

**(d)** The cylinder begins to slip when $\tan\theta_{\text{min}} = 3\mu_s$, so:
$$\theta_{\text{min}} = \tan^{-1}(3\mu_s)$$

**Scoring rubric:**

- Part (a): 1 point for each correct force and direction
- Part (b): 1 point for each correct equation
- Part (c): 2 points for correct moment of inertia, 2 points for deriving the condition
- Part (d): 2 points for the final expression

---

## Common Mistakes in AP Physics C Mechanics

1. **Confusing mass and weight.** Mass is in kg; weight is in Newtons ($W = mg$).

2. **Forgetting that friction does negative work.** When an object slides, friction opposes motion and removes mechanical energy from the system.

3. **Using $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ for non-constant acceleration.** This equation only works for constant acceleration.

4. **Sign errors in rotational dynamics.** Choose a consistent sign convention for torque and angular acceleration.

5. **Assuming all objects roll without slipping.** Check whether the friction is sufficient to prevent slipping.

6. **Confusing center of mass with geometric center.** For non-uniform objects, these may differ.

## Exam Tips

- Always draw a free-body diagram before writing equations
- For rotational problems, specify the axis of rotation
- Use conservation of energy when forces are conservative
- Check that your answer has correct units and reasonable magnitude
- For free-response problems, show all steps and box your final answer

## Biology (Q1–Q10)

### Q1, Cell Structure and Function

Which of the following best describes the function of the rough endoplasmic reticulum?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Lipid synthesis |
| B | Protein synthesis and modification |
| C | ATP production |
| D | DNA replication |
| E | Detoxification of drugs |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

The rough ER is studded with ribosomes and is the site of protein synthesis and initial modification (glycosylation). The smooth ER (A) synthesises lipids. Mitochondria (C) produce ATP. The nucleus (D) is the site of DNA replication.

`easy`1 mark

---

### Q2, Cellular Respiration

During oxidative phosphorylation, electrons are passed through the electron transport chain to:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Glucose |
| B | Pyruvate |
| C | Oxygen |
| D | Carbon dioxide |
| E | NAD+ |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

In oxidative phosphorylation, electrons are passed along the electron transport chain and ultimately accepted by oxygen, the final electron acceptor, forming water. This creates the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase.

`medium`1 mark

### Q3, Genetics and Gene Expression

In eukaryotic gene regulation, which of the following is most directly responsible for activating transcription of a specific gene?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Methylation of DNA |
| B | Binding of transcription factors to the promoter |
| C | Acetylation of histones |
| D | Degradation of mRNA |
| E | Splicing of pre-mRNA |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

Transcription factors bind to the promoter region and recruit RNA polymerase, directly activating transcription. Histone acetylation (C) generally facilitates transcription by relaxing chromatin but does not directly activate specific genes.

`medium`1 mark

### Q4, Evolution

Which of the following provides the strongest evidence for evolution?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Artificial selection by humans |
| B | The fossil record showing transitional forms |
| C | DNA sequence similarities across species |
| D | All of the above |
| E | The theory of natural selection |

**Correct: D** (index 3)

All of these provide evidence for evolution. Artificial selection demonstrates that selection produces rapid change. Fossils show gradual transitions. DNA similarities indicate common ancestry. The convergence of multiple independent lines of evidence is what makes evolution so well-supported.

`medium`1 mark

### Q5, Ecology

In an ecosystem, the concept of a "trophic cascade" refers to:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Energy transfer between trophic levels |
| B | A top predator indirectly affecting lower trophic levels |
| C | The decomposition of dead organisms |
| D | Nutrient cycling through the ecosystem |
| E | Primary succession in a habitat |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

A trophic cascade occurs when a top predator suppresses the abundance of herbivores, which in turn allows producers to flourish. The classic example is the reintroduction of wolves in Yellowstone, which reduced elk grazing and allowed vegetation recovery.

`medium`1 mark

### Q6, Human Physiology

The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) regulates:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Blood glucose levels |
| B | Blood pressure and fluid balance |
| C | Calcium homeostasis |
| D | Thyroid hormone levels |
| E | Immune response |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

The RAAS is activated when blood pressure drops. Renin triggers the production of angiotensin II, which constricts blood vessels and stimulates aldosterone release, increasing sodium and water reabsorption. This raises blood pressure and restores fluid balance.

`medium`1 mark

### Q7, Molecular Biology

A mutation that changes a single nucleotide in a coding region but does not change the amino acid produced is called:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | A frameshift mutation |
| B | A nonsense mutation |
| C | A silent mutation |
| D | A missense mutation |
| E | An insertion |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

A silent mutation changes the DNA sequence but not the amino acid, due to the redundancy of the genetic code. A missense mutation (D) changes one amino acid to another. A nonsense mutation (B) introduces a premature stop codon.

`easy`1 mark

### Q8, Plant Biology

Guard cells regulate the opening and closing of stomata by:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Changing the pH of the leaf |
| B | Accumulating or losing potassium ions, which changes their shape |
| C | Producing abscisic acid in response to light |
| D | Directly absorbing carbon dioxide from the air |
| E | Dividing to create new stomatal pores |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

Guard cells open stomata by accumulating K+ ions, which lowers their water potential, causing water to enter by osmosis. The cells become turgid and bow apart, opening the pore. When K+ is lost, the cells become flaccid and the pore closes.

`medium`1 mark

### Q9, Immunology

Which of the following is characteristic of the adaptive immune response but NOT the innate immune response?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Rapid response to infection |
| B | Use of physical barriers |
| C | Immunological memory |
| D | Phagocytosis by neutrophils |
| E | Inflammation |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

Immunological memory is unique to the adaptive immune system. After an initial exposure, memory B and T cells enable a faster, stronger response upon re-exposure. This is the basis of vaccination. All other options are features of innate immunity.

`medium`1 mark

### Q10, Biochemistry

Which of the following is a characteristic of competitive enzyme inhibitors?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | They bind irreversibly to the enzyme |
| B | They increase Vmax |
| C | They increase the apparent Km |
| D | They bind to an allosteric site |
| E | They cannot be outcompeted by substrate |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

Competitive inhibitors compete with substrate for the active site, increasing the apparent Km (lowering apparent affinity) without changing Vmax. They can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration. Non-competitive inhibitors decrease Vmax.

`medium`1 mark

## Chemistry (Q11–Q20)

### Q11, Atomic Structure

Which of the following elements has the highest electronegativity?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Sodium |
| B | Silicon |
| C | Phosphorus |
| D | Chlorine |
| E | Argon |

**Correct: D** (index 3)

Electronegativity generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. Chlorine has the highest electronegativity of the listed elements (3.0 on the Pauling scale). Argon, being a noble gas, does not typically form bonds.

`easy`1 mark

### Q12, Chemical Bonding

In molecular orbital theory, which of the following species is paramagnetic?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | N2 |
| B | O2 |
| C | F2 |
| D | Ne2 |
| E | He2 |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

O2 has two unpaired electrons in its antibonding pi* orbitals, making it paramagnetic. This is one prediction of MO theory that Lewis structures fail to explain. N2 and F2 are diamagnetic.

`medium`1 mark

### Q13, Stoichiometry

What volume of 0.10 M HCl is required to neutralise 25.0 mL of 0.20 M NaOH?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 12.5 mL |
| B | 25.0 mL |
| C | 50.0 mL |
| D | 100.0 mL |
| E | 5.0 mL |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

At the equivalence point, moles of HCl = moles of NaOH: 0.10 x V = 0.20 x 25.0, so V = (0.20 x 25.0) / 0.10 = 50.0 mL.

`easy`1 mark

### Q14, Thermodynamics

For a reaction to be spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure, which condition must be met?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | delta H > 0 and delta S > 0 |
| B | delta H < 0 and delta S > 0 |
| C | delta G > 0 |
| D | delta G < 0 |
| E | Both B and D |

**Correct: E** (index 4)

A reaction is spontaneous when delta G < 0. Since delta G = delta H - T*delta S, the most favourable conditions are delta H < 0 (exothermic) and delta S > 0 (increase in entropy), which always give delta G < 0.

`medium`1 mark

### Q15, Kinetics

According to collision theory, which of the following will increase the rate of a reaction?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Decreasing the temperature |
| B | Adding a catalyst |
| C | Decreasing the concentration of reactants |
| D | Using a larger container |
| E | Removing the products |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, increasing the rate without being consumed. Lowering temperature (A) and concentration (C) decrease the rate. A larger container (D) decreases concentration.

`easy`1 mark

### Q16, Equilibrium

For the equilibrium 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), increasing the pressure will:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Shift equilibrium to the left |
| B | Shift equilibrium to the right |
| C | Have no effect on equilibrium |
| D | Decrease the value of Kc |
| E | Increase the concentration of SO2 |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. The left side has 3 moles; the right side has 2 moles. Equilibrium shifts to the right to reduce pressure. Kc only changes with temperature.

`medium`1 mark

### Q17, Acids and Bases

Which of the following is a buffer solution?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | HCl and NaCl |
| B | CH3COOH and CH3COONa |
| C | NaOH and NaCl |
| D | HNO3 and KOH |
| E | Pure water |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

A buffer consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid). CH3COOH (weak acid) and CH3COONa (its conjugate base) form a buffer. Strong acid + salt (A), strong base + salt (C), and strong acid + strong base (D) are not buffers.

`medium`1 mark

### Q18, Electrochemistry

In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Cathode |
| B | Anode |
| C | Salt bridge |
| D | Negative terminal only |
| E | Both electrodes |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

In both galvanic and electrolytic cells, oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Remember: An Ox (anode oxidation), Red Cat (reduction at cathode).

`easy`1 mark

### Q19, Organic Chemistry

Which of the following is the correct IUPAC name for CH3CH(OH)CH3?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 1-propanol |
| B | 2-propanol |
| C | Propanal |
| D | Propanone |
| E | Ethanol |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

The OH group is on carbon 2 of a 3-carbon chain, so the name is 2-propanol (isopropanol). 1-propanol has the OH on carbon 1. Propanal and propanone contain carbonyl groups, not hydroxyl groups.

`easy`1 mark

### Q20, Nuclear Chemistry

In beta-minus decay, a neutron in the nucleus is converted into:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | A proton and an electron |
| B | A proton and a positron |
| C | Two protons |
| D | An alpha particle |
| E | A gamma ray |

**Correct: A** (index 0)

In beta-minus decay, a neutron converts into a proton and an electron (beta particle). The electron is emitted, and the atomic number increases by 1 while the mass number stays the same. Beta-plus decay produces a positron (B).

## Physics (Q21–Q30)

### Q21, Kinematics

A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20 m/s. Ignoring air resistance, what is the maximum height reached? (g = 10 m/s^2)

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 10 m |
| B | 20 m |
| C | 40 m |
| D | 2 m |
| E | 100 m |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

At maximum height, v = 0. Using v^2 = u^2 - 2gh: 0 = 20^2 - 2(10)h, so 400 = 20h, giving h = 20 m.

`easy`1 mark

### Q22, Newton's Laws

A 5 kg object is subject to two forces: 10 N to the right and 3 N to the left. What is the acceleration?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 0.6 m/s^2 right |
| B | 1.4 m/s^2 right |
| C | 2.6 m/s^2 right |
| D | 5.0 m/s^2 right |
| E | 7.0 m/s^2 right |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

Net force = 10 - 3 = 7 N to the right. By Newton's second law: a = F/m = 7/5 = 1.4 m/s^2.

`easy`1 mark

---

### Q23, Work and Energy

A 2 kg block slides down a frictionless ramp from a height of 5 m. What is its speed at the bottom? (g = 10 m/s^2)

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 5 m/s |
| B | 10 m/s |
| C | 50 m/s |
| D | 25 m/s |
| E | 100 m/s |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

By conservation of energy: mgh = (1/2)mv^2, so v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 5) = sqrt(100) = 10 m/s.

`easy`1 mark

### Q24, Momentum

A 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg object. After the collision, they stick together. What is the final velocity?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 1 m/s |
| B | 3 m/s |
| C | 4 m/s |
| D | 12 m/s |
| E | 16 m/s |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

By conservation of momentum: m1*v1 + m2*v2 = (m1 + m2)*v_final. (3)(4) + (1)(0) = (4)*v_final, so 12 = 4*v_final, giving v_final = 3 m/s.

`easy`1 mark

### Q25, Circular Motion

A car of mass 1000 kg travels around a circular track of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 20 m/s. What is the centripetal force?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 400 N |
| B | 4,000 N |
| C | 8,000 N |
| D | 20,000 N |
| E | 100,000 N |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

F = mv^2/r = (1000)(20^2)/50 = (1000)(400)/50 = 400,000/50 = 8,000 N.

`medium`1 mark

### Q26, Gravitation

If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force between them:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Doubles |
| B | Halves |
| C | Quadruples |
| D | Becomes one-quarter |
| E | Remains the same |

**Correct: D** (index 3)

By Newton's law of gravitation, F = Gm1m2/r^2. If r doubles, F becomes Gm1m2/(2r)^2 = Gm1m2/(4r^2) = F/4.

`medium`1 mark

### Q27, Oscillations

A mass-spring system has a spring constant of 100 N/m and a mass of 0.25 kg. What is the period of oscillation?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 0.05 s |
| B | 0.10 s |
| C | 0.314 s |
| D | 3.14 s |
| E | 6.28 s |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k) = 2*pi*sqrt(0.25/100) = 2*pi*sqrt(0.0025) = 2*pi*0.05 = 0.314 s (approximately pi/10).

`medium`1 mark

### Q28, Rotational Motion

A solid sphere rolls without slipping down an incline. At the bottom, what fraction of its kinetic energy is rotational?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 2/7 |
| B | 5/7 |
| C | 1/2 |
| D | 2/5 |
| E | 3/5 |

**Correct: A** (index 0)

For a solid sphere, I = (2/5)mr^2. With v = omega*r (rolling without slipping), KE_rot = (1/2)I*omega^2 = (1/2)(2/5)mr^2*(v/r)^2 = (1/5)mv^2. KE_total = (1/2)mv^2 + (1/5)mv^2 = (7/10)mv^2. Fraction = (1/5)/(7/10) = 2/7.

`hard`1 mark

### Q29, Fluid Mechanics

According to Bernoulli's principle, where the speed of a fluid increases, the pressure:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Increases |
| B | Decreases |
| C | Remains constant |
| D | Depends on temperature |
| E | Oscillates |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

Bernoulli's principle states that for an incompressible, non-viscous fluid in steady flow, an increase in speed occurs simultaneously with a decrease in pressure. This explains lift on airplane wings and the curve of a spinning ball.

`easy`1 mark

### Q30, Waves and Optics

A double-slit experiment uses light of wavelength 500 nm. The slit separation is 0.1 mm and the screen is 2 m away. What is the fringe spacing?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 0.1 mm |
| B | 1 mm |
| C | 10 mm |
| D | 100 mm |
| E | 1 mm |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

Fringe spacing = lambda*D/d = (500 x 10^-9)(2)/(0.1 x 10^-3) = (10^-6)/(10^-4) = 10^-2 m = 10 mm.

What is the derivative of f(x) = x^3 * e^x?

What is the integral of 2x / (1 + x^2) dx?

### Q35, Definite Integrals

What is the definite integral from 0 to pi of sin(x) dx?

| --- | --- |

| B | 1 |
| C | 2 |
| D | pi |
| E | -2 |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

Integral of sin(x) = -cos(x). Evaluating from 0 to pi: [-cos(pi)] - [-cos(0)] = [-(-1)] - [-1] = 1 + 1 = 2.

### Q36, Applications of Derivatives

For f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2, at which value of x does f have a local maximum?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | x = -1 |
| B | x = 0 |
| C | x = 1 |
| D | x = 2 |
| E | x = 3 |

**Correct: A** (index 0)

f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x^2 - 1) = 3(x-1)(x+1). Critical points at x = 1 and x = -1. f''(x) = 6x. f''(-1) = -6 < 0, so x = -1 is a local maximum. f''(1) = 6 > 0, so x = 1 is a local minimum.

`medium`1 mark

### Q37, Related Rates

A circle's radius increases at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area increasing when r = 5 cm?

| # | Option |

| B | 20 pi cm^2/s |
| C | 25 pi cm^2/s |
| D | 50 pi cm^2/s |
| E | 100 pi cm^2/s |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

A = pi*r^2. dA/dt = 2*pi*r * dr/dt = 2*pi*5*2 = 20 pi cm^2/s.

The volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region under y = x from x = 0 to x = 1 about the x-axis is:

### Q39, Series

What is the sum of the infinite geometric series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ...?

| --- | --- |
| A | 1 |
| B | 1.5 |
| C | 2 |
| D | Infinity |
| E | 0.5 |

This is a geometric series with a = 1 and r = 1/2. Since |r| < 1, the sum = a/(1-r) = 1/(1-1/2) = 1/(1/2) = 2.

### Q40, Differential Equations

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | y = 2x + C |
| B | y = Ce^(2x) |
| C | y = 2e^x |
| D | y = e^(2x) |
| E | y = Ce^(x/2) |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

Separating variables: dy/y = 2 dx. Integrating: ln|y| = 2x + C. Exponentiating: y = e^(2x+C) = e^C * e^(2x) = Ce^(2x).

`medium`1 mark

---

## Statistics (Q41–Q50)

### Q41, Descriptive Statistics

A data set has values: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. What is the mean?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 4 |
| B | 4.5 |
| C | 5 |
| D | 5.5 |
| E | 6 |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

Mean = (2+4+4+4+5+5+7+9)/8 = 40/8 = 5.

`easy`1 mark

---

### Q42, Probability

Two independent events A and B have P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 0.12 |
| B | 0.7 |
| C | 0.3 |
| D | 0.4 |
| E | 0.7 |

**Correct: A** (index 0)

For independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) *P(B) = 0.3* 0.4 = 0.12.

`easy`1 mark

---

### Q43, Distributions

In a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of data falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 68% |
| B | 95% |
| C | 99.7% |
| D | 50% |
| E | 75% |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

The empirical rule states: approximately 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, and 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean.

`easy`1 mark

---

### Q44, Sampling

Which sampling method is most likely to produce a biased sample of students at a university?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Simple random sample |
| B | Stratified random sample |
| C | Convenience sample |
| D | Systematic sample |
| E | Cluster sample |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

A convenience sample uses the most easily accessible individuals, which introduces selection bias. For example, surveying only students in the library excludes those who study elsewhere. Random sampling methods (A, B, D, E) reduce bias.

`easy`1 mark

---

### Q45, Hypothesis Testing

In a hypothesis test, a p-value of 0.03 means:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true |
| B | There is a 3% chance of observing the data if the null hypothesis is true |
| C | There is a 97% chance the alternative hypothesis is true |
| D | The effect size is 0.03 |
| E | The sample size is 3% of the population |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the observed data, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

`medium`1 mark

---

### Q46, Confidence Intervals

A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is (10, 16). Which interpretation is correct?

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | 95% of the data falls between 10 and 16 |
| B | There is a 95% probability the population mean is between 10 and 16 |
| C | If we repeated the sampling many times, approximately 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean |
| D | 95% of samples will have means between 10 and 16 |
| E | The true mean is exactly 13 |

**Correct: C** (index 2)

A confidence interval is about the reliability of the method. A 95% CI means that if we repeated the experiment many times, approximately 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true population parameter.

`medium`1 mark

---

### Q47, Regression

In a linear regression model, the coefficient of determination (R-squared) measures:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | The slope of the regression line |
| B | The proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable |
| C | The correlation between the variables |
| D | The y-intercept of the regression line |
| E | The standard deviation of the residuals |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

R-squared measures the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s). An R-squared of 0.85 means 85% of the variation in Y is explained by the model.

`medium`1 mark

---

### Q48, Experimental Design

In a randomised controlled experiment, the control group:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Receives the treatment |
| B | Does not receive the treatment and serves as a comparison |
| C | Is always a placebo group |
| D | Must be the same size as the treatment group |
| E | Is selected by the researcher |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

The control group does not receive the experimental treatment and serves as a baseline for comparison. This allows researchers to determine whether the treatment has an effect. The control group may receive a placebo (C), but this is not always the case.

`easy`1 mark

---

### Q49, Chi-Squared Test

A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test is used to determine whether:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | Two quantitative variables are correlated |
| B | An observed distribution matches an expected distribution |
| C | Two population means are equal |
| D | A population proportion exceeds a threshold |
| E | Data are normally distributed |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

The chi-squared goodness-of-fit test compares observed frequencies to expected frequencies to determine whether the data fit a specific distribution. It is used for categorical data.

`medium`1 mark

---

### Q50, Type Errors

In hypothesis testing, a Type II error occurs when:

| # | Option |
| --- | --- |
| A | The null hypothesis is rejected when it is true |
| B | The null hypothesis is not rejected when it is false |
| C | The alternative hypothesis is rejected when it is true |
| D | The sample size is too small |
| E | The p-value is calculated incorrectly |

**Correct: B** (index 1)

A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive). A Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative). Reducing one type of error typically increases the other, holding sample size constant.

`medium`1 mark

## Cell Structure And Function
